title: Lipid nanoparticles for mRNA delivery
full_text:
Abstract
Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the most clinically advanced non-viral platform for mRNA delivery, exemplified by the COVID-19 vaccines. LNPs consist of four key components: ionizable lipids, helper phospholipids, cholesterol, and PEG-lipids. The ionizable lipid is the key determinant of potency, facilitating mRNA encapsulation and endosomal escape. Despite clinical success, LNPs have limitations: they primarily accumulate in the liver, and endosomal escape efficiency remains below 2% of internalized dose.

Introduction
Messenger RNA therapeutics require carriers that protect cargo from nucleases, enable cellular uptake, and release intact mRNA into the cytosol. We propose that multi-component LNPs achieve this through pH-dependent ionization of the lipid headgroup. Prior work (Semple et al., 2010) established ionizable lipids as safer than permanently cationic lipids. However, the exact molecular mechanism of endosomal membrane disruption remains poorly understood, limiting rational design of next-generation lipids.

Methods
LNPs were formulated by microfluidic mixing of an ethanolic lipid phase (ionizable lipid, DSPC, cholesterol, PEG-lipid at 50:10:38.5:1.5 mol%) with aqueous mRNA at N/P = 6. Particle size and PDI were measured by dynamic light scattering. Encapsulation efficiency was quantified by RiboGreen assay. In vitro transfection used HeLa and primary hepatocyte cultures with firefly luciferase mRNA. Endosomal escape was scored with a Gal8 recruitment assay. In vivo biodistribution used IV-injected LNPs in C57BL/6 mice with IVIS imaging at 6 h and 24 h. Controls included empty LNPs, naked mRNA, and MC3 reference LNPs. Each condition was run in biological triplicate.

Results
Mean hydrodynamic diameter was 78 ± 6 nm with PDI < 0.12 and encapsulation efficiency of 92%. Luciferase expression in hepatocytes was 15-fold higher than MC3-matched controls at 0.1 mg/kg. Gal8 recruitment indicated that less than 2% of encapsulated mRNA reached the cytosol, confirming endosomal escape as the major bottleneck. Liver-to-spleen luminescence ratio was 18:1 after IV dosing. PEG-lipid desorption over 24 h correlated with accelerated blood clearance on second dose (p < 0.01).

Discussion
These findings support the hypothesis that ionizable lipid pKa near 6.4 maximizes endosomal protonation while limiting surface charge in circulation. The protein corona acquired in serum redirects a fraction of particles to scavenger-receptor-rich tissues, which may explain residual extrahepatic signal. We argue that improving endosomal escape above 5% cytosolic delivery would unlock dose-sparing mRNA vaccines and enable non-hepatic gene editing. Structure-activity relationships linking lipid tail unsaturation to membrane fusion remain incompletely mapped.

Limitations
This study used rodent models and a single reporter mRNA; translation to large-animal toxicology and multi-dose human regimens is unproven. Endosomal escape quantification relies on a proxy assay and may underestimate true cytosolic delivery. Extrahepatic targeting was not systematically optimized beyond PEG-lipid tuning.

Conclusions
LNPs remain the leading non-viral mRNA platform, yet endosomal escape efficiency below 2% and hepatic tropism are unresolved barriers. Mechanism-focused lipid design and corona-aware formulation are high-priority experimental directions.

title: Endosomal escape of lipid nanoparticles: a mechanistic investigation
full_text:
Abstract
The mechanism by which lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) escape the endosome is not fully understood. Using a combination of fluorescence microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, and lipid mixing assays, we investigated the intracellular trafficking of LNPs in HeLa and DC2.4 cells. We observed rapid internalization via clathrin-mediated endocytosis, followed by accumulation in early endosomes. Using a newly developed probe, we show that ionizable-lipid protonation drives membrane contact and limited hexagonal-phase lipid mixing, yet most particles remain trapped.

Introduction
Cytosolic delivery is rate-limiting for LNP-mediated RNA therapeutics. We hypothesize that endosomal escape proceeds through transient membrane fusion rather than wholesale endosome rupture. Prior models assume hexagonal HII phase transition of ionizable lipids at low pH, but quantitative cryo-ET evidence in intact cells has been scarce. It is believed that helper phospholipids modulate curvature stress required for fusion pores.

Methods
LNPs encapsulating Cy5-labeled mRNA and ionizable lipid MC3 or SM-102 were prepared by T-junction mixing. Cells were incubated with LNPs for 5–120 min, fixed, and imaged by confocal microscopy and cryo-ET. Lipid mixing was measured with NBD/rhodamine FRET probes in endosome-mimetic liposomes at pH 5.5–7.4. Bafilomycin A1 blocked endosomal acidification as a negative control. At least 40 cells per condition were analyzed. Success criterion was detection of cytosolic Cy5 puncta above vehicle background.

Results
Uptake peaked within 30 min and was reduced 70% by clathrin inhibitor Pitstop-2. At pH 5.5, lipid mixing increased 4.2-fold versus pH 7.4 for SM-102 LNPs. Cryo-ET revealed membrane apposition events but intact endosomal limiting membranes in >90% of tomograms. Cytosolic mRNA signal remained below 2% of total internalized fluorescence at 2 h. Chloroquine co-treatment raised cytosolic signal to 6% but increased cytotoxicity (LDH +35%).

Discussion
Our results show that hexagonal-phase propensity correlates with lipid mixing yet is insufficient for efficient escape. We propose a multi-hit fusion-pore model in which repeated LNP–endosome contacts are required. The exact stoichiometry of ionizable lipid needed for a productive pore remains unknown. These data challenge the assumption that bulk membrane rupture is the dominant escape path and predict that lipids engineered for localized curvature at contact sites will outperform bulk HII formers.

Limitations
Imaging was limited to two cell lines; primary hepatocytes and in vivo endosomes may differ. FRET lipid mixing is an in vitro surrogate and may overestimate fusion competence. We did not resolve single-pore kinetics.

Conclusions
Endosomal escape of LNPs is rare, contact-localized, and poorly explained by bulk phase transition alone. Mechanism-guided lipid design and live-cell pore sensors are experimentally testable next steps.

title: Extrahepatic targeting of lipid nanoparticles in vivo
full_text:
Abstract
Clinical use of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) is limited by their predominant accumulation in the liver after systemic administration. We explored two strategies for extrahepatic targeting: ligand conjugation and tuning of lipid composition. Conjugation of anti-CD3 antibodies to LNP surfaces achieved T-cell-specific mRNA delivery with 60% transfection efficiency in vitro but only 15% in vivo due to opsonization and rapid clearance. SORT lipid doping shifted tropism partially toward lung and spleen.

Introduction
Hepatic tropism of LNPs is attributed to ApoE adsorption and LDL-receptor engagement. We propose that reducing ApoE binding while displaying tissue ligands can redirect LNPs without sacrificing endosomal escape. Alternative hypotheses emphasize PEG-lipid desorption kinetics and complement activation as dominant filters in vivo.

Methods
Antibody-conjugated LNPs used maleimide-PEG-lipid and thiolated anti-CD3. SORT formulations replaced 10–40% of ionizable lipid with permanently cationic DOTAP or anionic 18PA. Biodistribution used luciferase mRNA in BALB/c mice (n=5/group) with ex vivo organ luminescence at 6 h. Flow cytometry quantified immune-cell transfection. Controls: unconjugated LNP, isotype IgG-LNP, and PBS. Stop rule: >20% body-weight loss or ALT/AST >5× ULN.

Results
Liver luminescence fell from 85% of total organ signal (standard LNP) to 65% with optimized PEG-lipid and further to 48% with SORT-DOTAP 20%. Spleen signal rose 3.1-fold; lung signal rose 5.4-fold with SORT. Anti-CD3 LNPs transfected 15% of circulating CD3+ T cells in vivo versus 60% in vitro. Protein corona mass spectrometry showed enriched complement C3 on conjugated particles. Extrahepatic delivery remains elusive at therapeutically relevant doses without toxicity trade-offs.

Discussion
These experiments indicate that corona remodeling, not ligand density alone, gates extrahepatic access. We argue that passive SORT charge tuning is more reproducible than antibody conjugation for first-pass organ shift, whereas active ligands may require stealth corona engineering. The protein corona plays a critical role in LNP biodistribution and can nullify surface ligands. Predicted experiments: corona-fingerprint screens across lipid chemistries and Fc-silent ligand formats.

Limitations
Species differences in ApoE and complement may limit mouse-to-human translation. We did not measure long-term adaptive immune responses to conjugated proteins. Organ luminescence is a bulk proxy and does not prove cell-type specificity in parenchyma.

Conclusions
Partial extrahepatic retargeting is achievable via lipid composition and ligands, but corona-mediated clearance and residual hepatic uptake remain major barriers. Corona-aware design is a high-impact, testable research direction.

title: Combinatorial design of ionizable lipids for lipid nanoparticle delivery of mRNA
full_text:
Abstract
We report a combinatorial library of 120 ionizable lipids synthesized via Michael addition chemistry to identify novel lipid structures for mRNA delivery. The library varied alkyl tail length, amine headgroup chemistry, and linker composition. Top candidates were formulated into LNPs and screened for in vitro mRNA delivery in HeLa and Hep3B cells. The most potent lipids contained imidazole-based headgroups and unsaturated C16–C18 tails.

Introduction
Structure-activity relationships (SAR) for ionizable lipids remain incomplete outside a few clinical scaffolds. We hypothesize that imidazole headgroups buffer within the endosomal pH window and improve escape versus tertiary amines alone. It is thought that linker hydrolytic stability trades off potency against reactogenicity.

Methods
Lipids were synthesized in 96-well format and used without extensive purification for primary screens. LNPs encapsulated FLuc mRNA at N/P 6. Hit criteria: >10× luciferase vs MC3 at 50 ng/well and cell viability >80%. Secondary assays: pKa via TNS fluorescence, hemolysis at pH 5.5/7.4, and in vivo 0.05 mg/kg mouse liver expression. Negative controls: empty LNPs and non-ionizable analogs.

Results
Eight lipids exceeded MC3 in Hep3B; three retained activity in primary human hepatocytes. Lead lipid IL-47 showed pKa 6.35, 12-fold in vitro gain, and 4-fold liver luminescence gain in vivo. Hemolysis at pH 7.4 was <5%, rising to 28% at pH 5.5. Saturated tails reduced potency 3–8 fold. One hit failed in vivo despite strong in vitro signal, highlighting translation gaps.

Discussion
SAR suggests endosomal-buffering headgroups plus mono-unsaturation maximize potency. We propose that in vitro–in vivo discordance arises from differential corona formation, not intrinsic escape chemistry alone. Predicted experiments include corona proteomics on hit vs miss lipids and endosomal pH clamp assays.

Limitations
Library coverage is biased toward Michael-addition chemistries. In vivo work used a single mouse strain and one dose. Long-term toxicity and multi-dose pharmacokinetics were not assessed.

Conclusions
Combinatorial lipid design recovers potent ionizable scaffolds, but mechanism-linked assays are required to explain in vitro–in vivo gaps and guide non-hepatic applications.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 lipid nanoparticle systems for in vivo gene editing
full_text:
Abstract
Lipid nanoparticles enable non-viral delivery of Cas9 mRNA and gRNA for in vivo gene editing. We demonstrate editing in mouse liver hepatocytes after a single IV dose, with indel rates of 40% at the TTR locus. Off-target editing remained below detection in the surveyed sites, yet durable expression and immune responses to Cas9 protein remain concerns for repeat dosing.

Introduction
Viral vectors for CRISPR face cargo limits and immunogenicity. We propose that transient mRNA-LNP delivery restricts nuclease exposure and improves safety. However, efficient extrahepatic editing and multiplex gRNA co-delivery are not fully achieved with current LNPs.

Methods
Cas9 mRNA and chemically modified gRNA were co-encapsulated in MC3-class LNPs. Mice received 0.5–2.0 mg/kg total RNA. Editing was measured by NGS amplicon sequencing at 7 days. Controls: LNP with non-targeting gRNA, PBS, and AAV8-Cas9 reference. Cytokines were profiled at 6 h. Stop rules: ALT >10× ULN or overt morbidity.

Results
TTR indel frequency reached 40 ± 6% in bulk liver at 1 mg/kg. Serum TTR protein fell 70% at day 14. Off-target sites (n=8) showed <0.1% indels. Anti-Cas9 IgG was detectable after dose 2 in 3/5 animals. Spleen and lung editing remained <1%, confirming hepatic bias. Endosomal escape of dual RNA cargos was not independently quantified.

Discussion
LNP-CRISPR achieves therapeutically relevant hepatic editing after one dose. We argue that immune recognition of Cas9 and poor non-hepatic tropism are the primary barriers to broader use. Hybrid strategies (transient immunosuppression, tissue-SORT LNPs, or self-inactivating nucleases) are experimentally testable. The mechanism linking dual-cargo LNP composition to simultaneous Cas9+gRNA cytosolic delivery remains poorly characterized.

Limitations
Off-target survey was not genome-wide. Large-animal and human hepatocyte data are absent. Multiplex editing and base-editor LNPs were out of scope.

Conclusions
mRNA-LNP CRISPR is viable for liver targets; delivery barriers and adaptive immunity define the next experimental agenda for extrahepatic gene editing.

title: Circular RNA LNPs with orthogonal ionizable lipids for durable extrahepatic expression
full_text:
Abstract
Circular RNA (circRNA) encapsulated in LNPs shows extended protein expression versus linear mRNA in mice. We compare ionizable lipid formulations for circRNA cargo and find that endosomal escape efficiency, not circularization alone, limits durability. Hybrid designs co-delivering circRNA and regulatory siRNA are proposed but lack in vivo validation.

Introduction
circRNA resists exonuclease decay and may reduce dosing frequency. We hypothesize that LNP parameters optimized for linear mRNA are suboptimal for larger circRNA topologies. Prior work demonstrated multi-day expression, yet mechanism of improved durability remains controversial.

Methods
circRNA encoding erythropoietin was produced by permuted intron-exon splicing and formulated in SM-102-like LNPs with orthogonal ionizable lipids for extrahepatic SORT. Expression was tracked 14 days in mice. Controls: linear modified mRNA, empty LNP. RNase R treatment confirmed circularity. Endosomal escape used Gal8 assays in HepG2.

Results
circRNA-LNP maintained EPO above baseline through day 10 versus day 3 for linear mRNA at matched dose. Gal8 scores did not differ significantly between cargos, indicating escape parity. Increasing ionizable lipid mol% from 50 to 58 raised expression 2.1-fold but increased ALT 1.8-fold. Bifunctional circRNA–siRNA co-encapsulation achieved 35% packing of both cargos yet silenced off-target genes inconsistently. Lung-to-liver signal ratio rose 3.4-fold with SORT doping.

Discussion
Durability gains appear dominated by RNA stability, not superior escape. We propose that hybrid bifunctional ncRNA cargos need dedicated LNP architectures. Exact trafficking differences between circ and linear RNA inside endosomes remain unknown.

Limitations
Immunogenicity of circRNA splicing scars was not fully profiled. Extrahepatic durability beyond day 14 was not measured.

Conclusions
circRNA-LNPs extend expression windows, but delivery chemistry and hybrid ncRNA co-delivery are open experimental problems aligned with high-impact molecular engineering.

title: Hybrid nucleic acid nanostructures for programmable intracellular delivery
full_text:
Abstract
We designed hybrid nucleic-acid nanostructures that present siRNA warheads and CpG motifs on a DNA origami scaffold for programmable intracellular delivery. In macrophage cultures, the construct achieved 70% target knockdown while elevating IL-6 4-fold versus free CpG. Delivery into solid tumor cores remained limited without a nanoparticle carrier.

Introduction
Hybrid and bifunctional ncRNA concepts promise multi-pathway control, yet experimental systems rarely quantify trade-offs between silencing potency and innate activation. We propose that spatial display on origami controls TLR9 engagement independently of RISC loading.

Methods
Origami scaffolds were folded with 6 siRNA handles and 4 CpG overhangs. Transfection used Lipofectamine or LNP co-formulation. Readouts: qPCR knockdown, ELISA cytokines, cell viability. Controls: scrambled siRNA origami, CpG-only, free siRNA. n=4 biological replicates.

Results
Silencing reached 70% for model gene PLK1 at 20 nM scaffold. IL-6 and TNF rose significantly versus siRNA-only (p<0.01). LNP co-formulation improved uptake 3-fold but reduced CpG-driven IL-6 by 40%, suggesting lipid shielding of TLR ligands. Tumor spheroid penetration depth was <40 µm without targeting ligands.

Discussion
Bifunctional display works in vitro, but carrier choice reweights immune versus silencing arms. Mechanism of lipid shielding of CpG is not fully understood. Predicted gap: in vivo titration of silencing versus innate activation with section-grounded biodistribution.

Limitations
No in vivo efficacy arm. Origami stability in serum was only measured to 12 h.

Conclusions
Hybrid nucleic-acid nanostructures are experimentally tractable bifunctional platforms; delivery carriers and immune-silencing trade-offs define the key theory–experiment gaps.

title: Bifunctional ncRNA-mRNA co-delivery reveals interference between RISC loading and translation
full_text:
Abstract
Co-encapsulating siRNA and mRNA in one LNP can silence one pathway while expressing another, but we find molecular interference between RISC loading and mRNA translation. Bifunctional ncRNA–mRNA designs therefore need stoichiometry rules that current theory does not provide.

Introduction
We hypothesize that Ago2 competition and endosomal co-escape timing explain loss of dual activity. Prior work treated cargos as independent payloads.

Methods
LNPs co-loaded FLuc mRNA and siGFP at mass ratios 4:1 to 1:4. HeLa-GFP cells were assayed for luminescence and GFP knockdown at 24 h. Single-cargo LNPs and sequential dosing were controls. Polysome profiling estimated translation engagement.

Results
At 1:1 mass ratio, mRNA expression fell 55% versus mRNA-only while siRNA knockdown fell from 80% to 35%. Shifting to 4:1 mRNA-heavy restored expression but collapsed silencing. Endosomal escape fraction remained <2% for both arms. Ribosome occupancy on FLuc dropped when siRNA excess was high.

Discussion
Results show non-additive dual-cargo behavior. We propose RISC and translation compete for co-escaped RNA pools. Exact kinetic model remains unknown and is experimentally testable with timed photo-uncaging.

Limitations
One cell line; no in vivo dual-readout tumor model.

Conclusions
Bifunctional ncRNA–mRNA co-delivery is a real gap between hybrid-cargo theory and measured interference.

title: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles for RNA delivery: design, mechanism, and applications
full_text:
Abstract
Ionizable lipids are the central functional component of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) for RNA delivery. These lipids are positively charged at low pH (enabling RNA encapsulation) and neutral at physiological pH (reducing toxicity). The field has progressed from early cationic lipids to modern ionizable lipids such as DLin-MC3-DMA, SM-102, and ALC-0315. Key structure-activity relationships include the pKa window, tail unsaturation, and biodegradable linkers.

Introduction
Design rules for ionizable lipids are still largely empirical. We review mechanisms proposed for encapsulation, apoE-mediated uptake, and endosomal escape, and identify claims that lack direct experimental support.

Methods
This review synthesizes published LNP composition tables, TNS pKa measurements, and in vivo ED50 values across siRNA and mRNA cargos. Comparative tables normalize potency to mg/kg RNA.

Results
Clinical ionizable lipids cluster near pKa 6.2–6.5. Lipids outside 5.5–7.0 rarely achieve hepatic ED50 <0.1 mg/kg for siRNA. Biodegradable ester linkers reduce hepatic vacuolation in multi-dose studies. Quantitative cytosolic delivery fractions are rarely reported, limiting mechanistic meta-analysis.

Discussion
We argue that absence of standardized endosomal-escape assays is a critical theory–experiment gap. Predicted high-impact work includes open reference LNPs, shared escape metrics, and non-hepatic SAR panels.

Limitations
As a review, no new wet-lab data are presented. Publication bias may inflate apparent SAR clarity.

Conclusions
Ionizable lipid design is clinically validated yet mechanistically under-instrumented; standardized escape and corona assays would convert empirical craft into testable theory.
